A.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 7. It results from an error in splitting the $1.035 \text{ kg}$ mass or in dividing by the fat volume.

B.explanation: The fat mass of $0.0366 \text{ kg}$ in volume $4.00 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^{3}$ gives $\rho = 9.15 \times 10^{2} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

C.explanation: Slightly too large. It comes from rounding or from using total density $1035 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ incorrectly instead of conserving separate masses.

D.explanation: Greater than the density of fat-free milk. Full-fat milk is less dense than fat-free milk, so fat must be less dense than $1.040 \times 10^{3} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

hints: Notice the 4.00% is by volume in the $1.000 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^{3}$ sample, so work out the fat volume and the fat-free volume separately.
Connect total mass to component masses with $m = \rho V$: the $1.035 \text{ kg}$ equals mass of fat-free milk plus mass of fat.
Subtract the fat-free mass found from $1.040 \times 10^{3} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ to leave the fat mass, then divide by the small fat volume.
walkthrough: Find the two volumes from the 4.00% by volume. $V_{fat} = 0.0400 \times 1.000 \times 10^{-3} = 4.00 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^{3}$ and $V_{free} = 0.960 \times 1.000 \times 10^{-3} = 9.60 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{3}$.
Use $m = \rho V$ for the fat-free part. $m_{free} = 1.040 \times 10^{3} \times 9.60 \times 10^{-4} = 0.9984 \text{ kg}$.
Conserve mass for the mixture. $m_{fat} = m_{total} - m_{free} = 1.035 - 0.9984 = 0.0366 \text{ kg}$.
Calculate fat density. $\rho_{fat} = m_{fat} / V_{fat} = 0.0366 / 4.00 \times 10^{-5} = 915 \text{ kg m}^{-3} = 9.15 \times 10^{2} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ with unit check $\text{kg} / \text{m}^{3}$.
